title: Wide Independent Reading Across Genres
keyIdea: Reading widely means reading many kinds of text, not just many books: different genres (mystery, science fiction, historical fiction, fantasy), different forms (novels, short stories, poems, plays, non-fiction such as memoir), and books from different periods and cultures. Mix comfort reads with stretch reads that have a few words you must work at, and build the stamina to finish whole books with a little reading every day.
familyTip: Write down the last ten things you read, then label each one with its genre or form and roughly when it was written. If most labels are the same, pick your next book from a gap: a poem collection, a play, a memoir, or a novel from before 1914.

visual.caption: Which genre does each clue belong to? Drag each card into a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: name genres from first lines, widen a reading log, sort comfort and stretch pages, date four texts and plan your reading stamina.

kid: A genre is a kind of story or text. Mystery, science fiction, historical fiction and fantasy are genres. A form is the shape a text takes: a novel, a short story, a poem, a play or non-fiction. A memoir is non-fiction. It is the true story of the writer's own life.

Reading widely does not mean reading lots of the same thing. Thirty fantasy books is a lot of reading, but it is narrow. Wide reading means trying new genres and forms. It also means books from other times and other places.
Old books are worth it. Romeo and Juliet is from about 1595. Frankenstein came out in 1818. They show how people lived and thought, and many newer books borrow their ideas.

Choose some books that stretch you. A comfort read is easy and fun. A stretch read has a few tricky words that you can work out. If almost every line has a word you don't know, save that book for later. Whole books need stamina, so read a little every day.
adult: The Key Stage 3 English programme of study asks pupils to read a wide range of fiction and non-fiction. That includes whole books, short stories, poems and plays, with wide coverage of genres, periods, forms and authors. It names English literature from before 1914 and from today, two Shakespeare plays, and seminal world literature. It also asks pupils to choose and read books on their own for challenge, interest and enjoyment.

Useful terms: genre, form, convention, fiction and non-fiction, memoir, play script, period, independent reading, reading stamina. A rough guide to difficulty comes from vocabulary research: readers follow a text on their own when they know about 98 per cent of its words. At about 95 per cent they can follow it with some effort or help. Below that, meaning breaks down.

Common mistakes: counting volume as breadth, so a pile of books in one genre feels like wide reading; reading only comfort books, or giving up on a stretch book at the first hard word; thinking a memoir is fiction because it tells a story in the first person; and thinking older books, such as Frankenstein, began as films. Be careful not to treat the tricky-word count as a strict rule. Interest and background knowledge matter too.

In the lab you drag six opening lines onto their genres. Then you add books to a reading log that holds eight fantasy books until it covers five kinds. Next you check three pages for tricky words and sort them into comfort, stretch and not yet. After that you put four texts in their century and set pages per day to finish a 240-page novel in two weeks.

practice.prompt: “The study door was locked from the inside, and the key was still in his pocket.” Which genre does this opening suggest?
practice.hint: Is there a puzzle or a crime to solve?
practice.explain: A locked room with the key inside is a puzzle to solve, so this opening signals a mystery.

practice.prompt: Priya has read 20 fantasy novels this year and nothing else. Which choice makes her reading wider?
choices: a poetry collection, a play and a memoir
practice.hint: Wide means new kinds of text, not more of the same.
practice.explain: New forms and genres widen her reading. More fantasy adds books, but not breadth.

practice.prompt: A novel has {p} pages. You read {d} pages a day. How many days will it take to finish?
practice.hint: Divide the number of pages by the pages you read each day.

practice.prompt: A page has 50 words and you know all but {k} of them. How many words on the page do you know?
practice.hint: Take the tricky words away from the 50 words on the page.
practice.explain: 50 − {k} = {=50-k} words you know on the page.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a memoir?
choices: a writer's true account of their own childhood
a novel told by an invented narrator
practice.hint: A memoir is non-fiction about the writer's own life.
practice.explain: A memoir is a true account of the writer's own life, so it is non-fiction, even when it reads like a story.

pool.prompt: “By 2350, the last forest grew under a glass dome on Mars.” Which genre is this?
pool.hint: Look at the date and the place.
pool.explain: A future date and life on another planet signal science fiction.
Romeo and Juliet is from about 1595, Frankenstein from 1818 and Noughts & Crosses from 2001.

pool.prompt: A book has about 3 tricky words in every 50 that you can work out from context. What is it for you?
choices: a book you should give up on
pool.hint: Easy enough to follow, hard enough to grow?
pool.explain: A few tricky words you can work out make a stretch read: hard enough to grow, not too hard to follow.

pool.prompt: Why is reading 30 books in one genre not the same as reading widely?
choices: wide reading means many kinds of text, not just many books
it is, as long as you finish them all
pool.hint: Is it about how many, or how many kinds?
pool.explain: Wide reading means covering genres, forms and periods. Thirty books of one kind is a lot of reading, but narrow.

pool.prompt: You want to finish a {p}-page novel in {d} days. How many pages a day do you need?
pool.hint: Share the pages equally across the days.

pool.prompt: Why read a novel written 200 years ago?
choices: it shows how people lived and thought then, and later books build on it
it has nothing to say to readers now
pool.hint: Think about what older books show, and who borrowed from them.
pool.explain: Older books show other times and ideas, and many newer books borrow their plots, characters and themes.

pool.prompt: Which line is from a play script?
choices: Is anyone there? I wondered, alone.
pool.hint: Look for a speaker name and stage directions in brackets.
pool.explain: A play script puts the speaker's name first, with stage directions in brackets and no speech marks.

pool.prompt: You read {d} pages a day for {n} days. How many pages is that?
pool.hint: Multiply the pages per day by the number of days.
